catalog_quote: Koch 1997:285: "(SC10) Stress shift to second syllable: #'SS.. > #S'S.. Stress in Arandic is on the first syllable beginning with a consonant (i.e. (V)'CV). This reflects the second syllable of Pre-Arandic. It is possible that the shift of stress is related to the earlier strong stress on the first syllable, which occasioned the reduction of vowels in unstressed syllables." Koch 1997:271 (abbreviations): "Ant Antekerrepenhe". Breen 2001:55: "The most widespread stress rule in Arandic, usually stated: main stress falls on the first vowel that follows a consonant, does not have a simple statement in terms of conventional syllables, but is: stress falls on the second syllable with VC(C) syllables. Henderson (1990) found also that plural and reciprocal morphology is sensitive to whether stems are monosyllabic or disyllabic, but the rule is straightforward only with the VC(C) model." Breen 2001:55 (sec.4.1 Antekerrepenh): "This dialect, virtually extinct now, was originally analysed (Breen 1977) as a two-vowel language. ... Ant phonology[fn.21] is now regarded as similar to that of CAr, except that prepalatalised apicals are distinct from retroflexes"; fn.21: "Which, however, is based mainly on transcriptions done in the 1970s and needs revision in the light of my much greater experience with other Arandic languages." [scan renders 'VC(C)' as 'VCCC)'; letter-spacing in the Koch scan normalised.]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Arandic-wide rule, applied to Antekerrepenh by inclusion rather than by a dedicated statement: primary stress falls on the first vowel that is preceded by a consonant -- i.e. on the initial syllable of consonant-initial words and on the second syllable of vowel-initial words (most words are vowel-initial); onset-sensitive, otherwise fixed at the left edge.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated for Antekerrepenh. Koch 1997:279 only remarks historically that four-syllable words in many Australian languages carry penultimate secondary stress (pre-Arandic), not a synchronic Ant claim.
new_statements.exceptions: Breen 2001:56: Antekerrepenh (and Ayerrereng) pronounce a homorganic glide before word-initial /i/ or /u/, and one Ayerrereng speaker 'sometimes transferred the stress to this vowel' (possible change in progress). Breen 2001:53 (Central Arrernte): loss of the velar glide h leaves stress/length on the initial vowel (ahentye [a'ntje]), and younger CAr speakers shift stress to the initial vowel in surface VCV words. Blevins 2001:488 lists Antekerrepenh under 'Arandic (all with stress shift)', initial C-loss 'invariable', citing Hale 1962 and Koch 1997.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level main stress in citation forms; Breen frames the rule via VC(C) syllabification (Breen & Pensalfini 1999). No Antekerrepenh-specific stress sentence was found in any opened source; the dedicated primary description (Breen 1977 Phonetica; Breen 1982 IAD grammar ms) could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 'Andegerebinha' (ande1247, ISO adg) = Antekerrepenh(e) (Austlang C12), the nearly extinct easternmost Arandic dialect (Breen 1977 'Andegerebenha'; Koch 'Ant'). Breen 2001 treats it as a dialect within the Arrernte group whose phonology is 'similar to that of CAr [Central Arrernte, east2379/cent2403 area]'. Hale's 1960 'Antikiripinhi (Georgina River variety)' material is per Breen 2001:56 fn.22 actually Ayerrereng (ayer1246), a closely related but distinct variety; do not conflate. The stress statements quoted are Arandic-wide (aran1267), not elicited specifically for ande1247.

new_statements.quote: p.3: "Further evidence that all Arrernte words are vowel-initial comes from stress assignment and the prosody sensitivity of verbal plural and reciprocal morphology. In Arrernte, stress is assigned within a word to the first nucleus that is preceded by a consonant. Thus, if the word begins in a consonant, stress falls on the first vowel; if the word begins in a vowel, stress falls on the second nucleus (vowel) in that word. ... If consonant-initial words, such as those in (2c-d), are indeed underlyingly /e/-initial, then stress in Arrernte falls on the second syllable and is computed at some level where the initial /e/ is present." p.9 (Paman and Arandic areas): "stress (on polysyllables) on the second vowel or the first vowel following a consonant".

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing statements (Koch 1997:285 SC10 'Stress in Arandic is on the first syllable beginning with a consonant (i.e. (V)'CV)'; Breen 2001:55). The explicit rule on p.3 is stated for Arrernte (the Eastern/Central Arrernte varieties of Henderson & Dobson 1994, fn.21), a sister Arandic variety, not for Antekerrepenh itself; p.9 restates the outcome for the Arandic area as a whole, which covers Antekerrepenh. Adds the analytical point that under underlying initial /e/ the rule is plain second-syllable stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first vowel that is preceded by a consonant: initial syllable in consonant-initial words, second syllable in vowel-initial words ((V)'CV); under the authors' analysis that all words are underlyingly vowel-initial (initial /e/ unrealized), this is uniformly second-syllable stress. Stated for Arrernte and (p.9) as the shared outcome across the Arandic area via Koch's (1997) change 10 'Stress shift to second syllable'.
new_statements.exceptions: p.2: the optional utterance-final vowel [U] 'may be stressed on occasion, as when it is the only vowel in the utterance' (e.g. /mpe/ 'come on' [mba']). fn.5 p.4: Davis (1988) treated Western Arrernte as onset-sensitive stress; the authors say their analysis applies to Western Arrernte too. No Antekerrepenh-specific exception is given; Antekerrepenh is named only in App. B (p.23) for Breen's 1977 two-vowel (length) analysis, not for stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Breen & Pensalfini 1999 analyse 'Arrernte' = the Eastern/Central Arrernte varieties of Henderson & Dobson 1994 (fn.21 p.21; fn.5 says the analysis also applies to Western Arrernte). Antekerrepenh (ande1247) is mentioned only in Appendix B (p.23) as 'the closely related Antekerrepenh' re Breen's 1977 vowel analysis; no Antekerrepenh-specific stress statement. The stress rule is carried to Antekerrepenh via the Arandic-wide statement on p.9 (and Koch 1997 SC10 / Breen 2001 sec.4.1 already in the catalog).
